title: Microscopic Origin of Dephasing in Solids from First-Principles Electron-Phonon Interactions
abstract: Electron-phonon interactions provide a microscopic origin of effective dephasing in solids within real -time TDDFT via a time-domain Williams-Lax framework. In metals, Drude -like damping emerges from a single disordered configuration; in dielectrics, the same mechanism yields clean high-harmonic spectra without introducing ultrashort phenomenological dephasing times. Mapping supercell dynamics onto a primitive-cell density matrix reveals that dephasing is governed primarily by population dynamics (diagonal elements) rather than by the decay of off-diagonal coherence.
summary: This work microscopically investigates how electron-phonon coupling causes dephasing in crystalline solids using real-time TDDFT. By comparing supercell and primitive-cell calculations, the authors demonstrate that damping arises mainly from population dynamics rather than coherence decay. This provides a crucial theoretical refinement for modeling open quantum systems in condensed matter.
main_problem: The paper aims to determine the microscopic origin of dephasing (decoherence) in solids, specifically attributing it to electron-phonon interactions.
main_result: Dephasing is shown to be governed primarily by population dynamics (diagonal elements) rather than off-diagonal coherence decay when analyzed via a primitive-cell density matrix. Furthermore, supercell calculations naturally reproduce expected damping timescales without needing empirical parameters.
method: The study employs real-time Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory (rt-TDDFT) within the Williams-Lax formalism, propagating dynamics using supercells with displaced ionic positions.
model_or_system: The system is solid-state materials (metals like Al and dielectrics like Si), where electron dynamics are coupled to lattice vibrations (phonons). The analysis compares results from large supercells versus the primitive cell representation.
key_observables: Time-dependent conductivity $\sigma(t)$, Drude-like damping, and spectral features in High-Harmonic Generation (HHG) spectra.
important_parameters: Phonon amplitudes sampled from zero-point motion; temperature (e.g., 300 K); supercell sizes ($2\times2\times2$ up to $4\times4\times4$).
main_assumptions: The adiabatic approximation is used, treating ionic positions as frozen during the femtosecond electron dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures compare $\sigma(t)$ for different supercell sizes in Al and Si, demonstrating exponential damping in larger cells. HHG spectra comparisons show that supercells yield cleaner harmonic peaks than primitive-cell calculations.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem using rt-TDDFT/Williams-Lax framework, analyzes linear response (conductivity) by comparing supercell vs. primitive cell results to pinpoint the source of damping, and extends the analysis to nonlinear responses like HHG.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, first-principles understanding of decoherence in solids, showing that complex many-body effects can emerge from simple population dynamics rather than just coherence decay, which is highly relevant for open quantum systems modeling.
